notes: Pashhur son of Malchijah is not Pashhur son of Immer, who struck Jeremiah in 20:1–2.
The Hebrew uses a form often transliterated Nebuchadrezzar here; this translation uses Nebuchadnezzar consistently for the same king.
“Them” can refer back to the weapons or to the besieging forces. The wording leaves the reference open.
“Life will be their plunder” means escaping with life as the gain from the conflict. The image recurs in 38:2 and 39:18.
“Your evil deeds” follows the marginal reading; the written form says “their evil deeds.”
vocabulary: The people associated here with Babylon's army and rule.
The royal dynasty descended from David.

sections.8: The way of life and the way of death

notes: The dead king and the departing king are contrasted. Verse 11 names the departing king Shallum; his exile, not merely his absence, is in view.

The wind “shepherds” the shepherds away. The following verb, rendered “how you will be pitied,” is difficult; it has also been understood as an ironic expression of favor or as groaning. The labor-pain image is clear.
Coniah is a shortened name of Jeconiah, named in 24:1. The signet ring carries the image of something close to the king and bearing his authority.
The passage mentions Coniah's offspring before calling him “childless.” Verse 30 specifies failure to continue the ruling line on David's throne; it need not deny that he had children.
vocabulary: A person living among a people without belonging to its native family or landholding structure.
A ring bearing a seal used to authenticate documents or possessions.

sections.10: The king who will not return

notes: The same Hebrew root connects the shepherds' failure to “attend” to the flock, the warning that God will “attend” to them, and the promise that none will be “missing.”

“Branch” is a growing shoot and an image for the promised Davidic ruler. The name “The LORD is our righteousness” is also given to Jerusalem in 33:16; the translation does not resolve its later theological interpretation.
The Hebrew changes to “I drove them” within the quoted oath. That change of person is retained.
“His word” follows the marginal reading. The written form at the second occurrence is “my word.” The council is the setting of authorized hearing and speaking in verses 18–22.
The Hebrew question is compressed and difficult. The translation supplies a verbal connection while retaining the question about the prophets' deceptive hearts.
The prophets claim to utter a declaration, the formula used for an authoritative oracle. The Hebrew does not repeat the divine name within their claim here.

“Burden” can name a prophetic message and also a load to carry. Verse 33 follows the Hebrew word division “What burden?”; redividing the consonants gives “You are the burden.” Verse 39 is also difficult: the pointed verb suggests forgetting, while the accompanying form suggests lifting or carrying. “I will lift you up” would continue the burden wordplay. These alternatives remain matters for review.
vocabulary: A bitter plant, used here as an image of the prophets' bitter fate.
A divine title evoking command over armies or heavenly forces; “hosts” means assembled forces.
Both a load and, in prophetic usage, an oracle; the double sense drives this exchange.

notes: The second group of skilled workers is traditionally called smiths or locksmiths; the precise occupational range is uncertain.

The favorable figs represent people already deported. The bad figs represent Zedekiah and those remaining in the land or living in Egypt. The comparison does not equate remaining at home with divine approval.
vocabulary: Recurring images of restoration, paired here with the reversal of tearing down and uprooting.

notes: The twenty-three years describe Jeremiah's speaking up to this address. The seventy years describe the nations' service to Babylon and the time before Babylon is called to account.

The list retains the hair-clipping practice and the name Zimri without assigning uncertain modern identities. Sheshach represents Babylon by substituting letters paired from opposite ends of the Hebrew alphabet.
The phrase translated “slaughter and scattering” is difficult. The text places the shepherds' downfall beside a precious vessel falling; it does not explain every part of the comparison.
“The fury of the oppressor” follows the pointed Hebrew. A reading involving a destroying sword is also possible with a different textual understanding; the final reference to burning anger is clear.
vocabulary: A severe expression of setting people or things apart for destruction; the violence is not merely loss of influence.
A cup whose drinking represents undergoing the announced judgment.

notes: The repeated verb “relent” concerns the announced disaster. The passage presents the people's turning and God's relenting as real possibilities, without explaining them through a later doctrinal scheme.
The marginal reading gives the short name Micah; the written form is Micaiah. The elders cite the earlier prophet's warning as a precedent.
Uriah's death is set beside Jeremiah's protection. The account does not promise every truthful prophet the same outcome.
vocabulary: An earlier sanctuary location invoked here as a warning about the temple's fate.
The killing of someone not guilty of the offense used to justify the killing, bringing bloodguilt on those responsible.

notes: The pinned Hebrew names Jehoiakim in verse 1, but verses 3 and 12 name Zedekiah, as does 28:1. The discrepancy is preserved rather than silently replacing the heading's king.
“His son and his grandson” preserves the stated dynastic sequence. The text is not expanded into a list of historical rulers.
The Hebrew literally lists “your dreams” among the sources of misleading guidance, though the surrounding list names people.
The promise concerns the furnishings still in Jerusalem, not an immediate return of the vessels already taken. The repeated introductions keep that distinction in view.
vocabulary: A bar and straps used to harness working animals; here a physical sign of subjection to Babylon.
The large water basin among the temple furnishings, not a geographical sea.

notes: Hananiah speaks in the fifth month and dies in the seventh month of the same year. His promised two-year return and Jeremiah's this-year warning have different deadlines.
Jeremiah's “Amen” expresses a wish that the promised return would happen. His following words still challenge whether Hananiah has been sent.
The Hebrew says “you have made” iron yoke bars. The action remains addressed to Hananiah; verse 14 then speaks of God's imposition of the iron yoke.
vocabulary: An expression of assent or desire: “May it be so.”

notes: The word rendered “court officers” can also designate eunuchs. The queen mother is distinguished from the king's wife.
The promise addresses the exiled community. The seventy years are “for Babylon.” The repeated word shalom links the city's well-being in verse 7 with the promised well-being in verse 11.
The unusual causative form can mean dreams the audience encourages others to dream; it can also be understood as dreams they themselves dream.
The Hebrew moves from “they did not listen” to “you did not listen,” drawing the exiled hearers into the accusation.

Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah are prophets in exile, not the kings bearing those names. The source's written/read difference in verse 23 is rendered according to the reading “the one who knows.”

Shemaiah's letter accuses Jeremiah of acting as a mad prophet. “Madman” belongs to that hostile speaker's claim. The second restraint in verse 26 is a rare word, probably a neck restraint; its exact construction is uncertain.
vocabulary: Shalom can include peace, safety, and communal welfare, not only the absence of fighting.
An expression of reversal and recovery that includes return from exile in this setting.

sections.4: Build, plant, and seek the city’s well-being
sections.15: Warnings at home and in Babylon

notes: The Hebrew moves between “your neck,” “him,” and “they.” Jacob or Israel remains the people addressed. “David their king” is retained without substituting an interpretive identification.
The poem moves from a wound called incurable to promised healing. Both the severe accusation and the reversal are retained.
“Pledge his own heart” is a striking expression of committing or risking oneself in approaching God. The preceding line makes the ruler's approach possible through God's invitation.
These lines closely echo 23:19–20. The storm description differs, but the completion of God's purpose and the promise of later understanding recur.
vocabulary: The elevated site on which a town stood, including the remains of earlier settlement.
A recurring covenant formula expressing the relationship promised to the community.

notes: The final phrase of verse 2 is compressed: Israel may be going to find rest, or the speaker may be going to give Israel rest. “From far away” in verse 3 may also mean “long ago”; “drawn you with steadfast love” can be understood as continuing steadfast love toward Israel.
The source says “Save your people,” a plea, and “with pleas for mercy,” language of supplication. Neither expression is silently replaced with a statement of completed rescue or consolation.
Rachel and Ephraim give the community's grief family voices. Verse 19 can be read “after I turned back” or “after I turned away.” Striking the thigh is a gesture of grief or remorse.
Verse 21 follows the marginal “you went,” addressed to feminine Israel. “A woman will surround a man” in verse 22 is an obscure image; the translation leaves its action and gender contrast intact.

The new covenant is promised to Israel and Judah. “I was their husband” in verse 32 can also express being their master. The Hebrew wording is retained; the note does not decide later interpretations of the covenant.

“Coming” in verse 38 is supplied by the marginal reading. Verses 39–40 also follow the marginal readings “measuring line” and “fields.” The city boundaries include the valley of corpses and ashes rather than avoiding its description.
vocabulary: A feminine personification of the people, addressed as a young woman.
Hebrew torah: authoritative teaching, including the covenant's requirements.

sections.35: The order of creation and the rebuilt city

notes: Hanamel is identified as Jeremiah's cousin in verses 7–9. Verse 12 uses the word normally meaning “uncle”; “kinsman” preserves the family relationship while this discrepancy remains visible here.
The wording distinguishes sealed and open documents. It does not fully describe the physical arrangement of the copies. The earthenware jar is intended to preserve them.

“Too difficult” can also be rendered “too wonderful.” The prayer retains both abundant steadfast love and the image of repaying fathers' guilt into their children's laps, alongside the individual accountability language in chapter 31.

Literally, they “caused their sons and daughters to pass over to Molech.” In this sacrificial setting the expression concerns offering children, not ordinary dedication; the violence is also explicit in 19:5.
vocabulary: A relative's claim to recover or purchase family property.
A unit of weight for the silver payment; the text describes weighed silver, not seventeen minted coins.
The lowland or foothill region and the southern region, named alongside the hill country.

notes: Verse 2 leaves the object of “does,” “shapes,” and “establishes” unstated. Verses 4–5 are syntactically difficult; the reading here connects the demolished houses with defense against siege, followed by their filling with bodies.

The returning wedding and thanksgiving sounds reverse earlier silence. The righteous Branch recalls 23:5, but in verse 16 the name “The LORD is our righteousness” belongs to Jerusalem, not directly to the ruler.
The “two clans” may refer to Israel and Judah or to the royal and priestly lines just discussed. The main text does not choose between them. Verse 26 follows the marginal causative “restore.”
vocabulary: The Hebrew image is of things fortified or inaccessible; the promise concerns what the speaker will disclose.
Priests identified with Levi's lineage; the promise here concerns continuing service before God.

notes: The text speaks of funeral burnings but does not name what is burned. It should not be taken as an explicit statement that the body is cremated.
The people actually freed enslaved men and women, then forcibly enslaved them again. The resulting “freedom” to sword, plague, and famine is a bitter reversal of their broken pledge.
The source retains both “at the end of seven years” and “served you six years.” The translation does not replace either number to simplify their relationship.
Passing between the cut calf's pieces accompanies the covenant. The threatened fate of the covenant breakers is set beside that of the animal.
vocabulary: A binding commitment; here a public pledge made before God to release enslaved people.

notes: The chapter uses both Jonadab and the longer Hebrew form Jehonadab for the same ancestor. Jonadab is used consistently here. His family's obedience is the comparison; the text does not issue their lifestyle rules to everyone.
War explains why the tent-dwelling family is now in Jerusalem. “Stand before me” in the closing promise expresses enduring access or service without specifying a new priestly office.
vocabulary: Live in a land without the standing of its native landholding families.

notes: The command to write comes in Jehoiakim's fourth year; the dated public reading occurs in his fifth year, in the ninth month. Both dates are retained.
Jeremiah says he is restricted or prevented from going to the temple. The precise cause is not stated here.
The king is identified elsewhere in the account as the one who burned the scroll. Three officials protest; their action is preserved alongside the lack of fear described in verse 24.
The replacement scroll contains the earlier words and additional words. The text does not present it as merely a duplicate.
vocabulary: Sections of writing on a scroll, cut off as they are read.
A container for burning fuel to provide heat.

sections.1: The words written on a scroll

notes: The purpose of Jeremiah's journey is uncertain; the verb can concern receiving a share or withdrawing. The term translated “cells” in verse 16 is rare, so the exact prison layout is uncertain.
The king seeks a private word but Jeremiah repeats the warning. The resulting change is a less severe place of confinement and a daily ration, not acquittal or freedom.
vocabulary: An enclosed area associated with the royal guard, used here to hold Jeremiah.

sections.17: A private question and a plea

notes: Jucal is the shorter form of Jehucal in 37:3. The term rendered “eunuch” for Ebed-melech can also mean a court officer; his Cushite identity is explicit.
The pinned Hebrew says thirty men. The rags and cloth are padding between Jeremiah's body and the lifting ropes, an important practical detail in the rescue.

The women's mud image recalls Jeremiah's cistern. Verse 23 literally says “you will burn this city”; the active wording places responsibility for its burning on the king rather than using a passive sentence.
The final clause, “when Jerusalem was captured,” introduces the next account. It remains within this verse instead of becoming unbound text between chapters.
vocabulary: Surviving the disaster with one's life as the gain; compare 21:9 and 39:18.
A pit or reservoir intended to hold water; this one contains mud instead.

notes: The Babylonian names and titles are difficult to divide. Verse 3 follows the Masoretic grouping Samgar-nebo and Sarsekim; another division groups Nebo-sarsechim and treats Samgar as a title. Rab-mag is retained as an official title whose precise office is uncertain.
The account keeps the king's sons' killing, his blinding, deportation, and the grant of land to some of the poorest survivors distinct.
This message looks back to Jeremiah's confinement. Ebed-melech is promised survival, expressed again as life gained as plunder.
vocabulary: The rift-valley region toward which the king fled.
The Babylonian officer responsible here for deportations and Jeremiah's release.

notes: This account places Jeremiah in chains at Ramah before his release. It is not expanded to explain its relationship to 39:14. The opening of verse 5 is difficult; the translation takes it as speaking before Jeremiah turns to leave.
The officer's “you” in verse 3 is plural, addressing the people's conduct. Verse 8 follows the marginal name Ephai.
vocabulary: Seasonal produce gathered and stored along with wine and oil.
